intro: You have heard the word Bible. Maybe you have seen one at home, in a library, or on a stand at a hotel. Maybe you have never opened one. In this unit you will find out what is inside. The Bible is not one book. It is a library of many books, and different groups keep different lists.

First you will learn how the library is built: its two big parts, its books, its chapters and verses, and the languages it was written in. You will learn to find any verse by its address. Then you will read the first five books, called the Torah, as one long story from the making of the world to the edge of a promised land.

This is a public school class. We study the Bible as literature and history. We say what the text says and how Jews and Christians read it. We never say it is true or false. By the end, you will be able to open a Bible, find your way, and explain its first big story to someone else.
bigQuestion: What is the Bible, and how does its first big story hold together?

timeline.t: The earliest Hebrew writing found so far dates from around this time
Many scholars think the Torah took its final shape around the time of the exile in Babylon
Jewish scholars in Egypt begin translating the Torah into Greek, later called the Septuagint
Jerome finishes a Latin Bible, the Vulgate, used in western churches for centuries
Stephen Langton divides the books into the chapters most Bibles still use
Gutenberg prints a Latin Bible, the first big book printed with movable type in Europe
William Tyndale prints an English New Testament
The King James Version is published in England
Chicago hosts the World's Parliament of Religions
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh

words.d: a collection of books that Jews and Christians treat as scripture; the name means "the books"
the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible, from Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
the Christian name for the books shared with the Hebrew Bible
the second part of the Christian Bible, about Jesus and his first followers
a small numbered part of a chapter, usually about one sentence
the same words moved from one language into another
the English Bible of 1611, now in the public domain
the first five books of the Bible; the Hebrew word means teaching
a binding promise with rules on both sides; the bond between God and Israel in the Torah
the Jewish holiday that remembers the night the Israelites left Egypt
the ten sayings that Exodus says were given at Mount Sinai
the words "Hear, O Israel" in Deuteronomy 6, said in Jewish daily prayer

test.q: What does the word Bible mean?
test.why: Bible comes from the Greek biblia, "the books."

test.q: How many books are in the Hebrew Bible, as Jews count them?
test.why: The Tanakh counts 24 books. Christian Bibles split some of them, so the same text becomes 39.

test.q: Which part of the Bible do Jews and Christians share?
choices: The Hebrew Bible, called the Old Testament by Christians
test.why: The Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament hold the same core books, counted differently.

test.q: In John 3:16, what does the 3 stand for?
test.why: The number before the colon is the chapter; the number after it is the verse.

test.q: In which language was the New Testament written?
test.why: The New Testament was written in Greek, the common language of the Roman world.

test.q: What is the King James Version?
test.why: King James of England ordered it in 1604 and it was finished in 1611.

test.q: Which name do Jews use for the first five books?
test.why: Torah means teaching. Christians also call these books the Pentateuch.

test.q: Which is the correct order of the first five books?
test.why: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy is the order of the story.

test.q: What does the rainbow mean in Genesis 9?
choices: A sign that a flood will not destroy the earth again
A sign that the tower would fall
A sign of the Ten Commandments
test.why: Genesis 9:13 calls the rainbow the token of a covenant between God and the earth.

test.q: Who is the man in Genesis 12 the story says was told to leave home for Canaan?
test.why: Genesis 12 tells of Abraham leaving his home for the land of Canaan.

choices: With Jacob's family living in Egypt
With the crossing of the sea
test.why: Genesis ends with Joseph's family settled in Egypt. Exodus picks up the story there.

test.q: What does the holiday of Passover remember?
choices: The giving of the law at Sinai
The end of the Torah reading
The night the Israelites left Egypt
test.why: Passover remembers the night of the last plague and the leaving of Egypt in Exodus 12.

test.q: Where does Exodus say the Ten Commandments were given?
test.why: Exodus 19 and 20 place the giving of the commandments at Mount Sinai.

test.q: Why does Numbers say the people wandered for forty years?
choices: They were afraid to enter Canaan after the spies' report
test.why: Numbers 13 and 14 say the people refused to go in out of fear, and so they wandered.

test.q: What happens to Moses at the end of Deuteronomy?
choices: He crosses the river into Canaan
He sees Canaan from Mount Nebo and dies there
test.why: Deuteronomy 34 says Moses saw the land from Mount Nebo but did not go in. Joshua led the people across.

write.prompt: Is the Torah more a book of stories or a book of rules? Cite two or three passages from this unit (for example Genesis 12:2, Exodus 20:8–12 and Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Say what each passage says, and explain how a Jewish reader and a Christian reader might each use it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Say "the text says" or "Jews believe" or "Christians believe"; do not say what is true.
Compare the two readings; do not judge which one is right.
Use the unit's words, like covenant, Torah and Tanakh, and show you know what they mean.
Keep your sentences short. One idea each.
